name: NEAR Intents
summary: A bug between the Omni withdrawal service and the intents contract let an attacker pull 3.87M USDT from a BNB Chain vault.
why: The flaw sat between off-chain withdrawal signing and the contract; the full root cause is not public.

name: Liquid Network
summary: A caching flaw in range-proof checks let unbacked L-BTC pass as real, and about 4,000 BTC left through normal peg-outs.
why: Feeding forged proofs to the validation code is a direct, replayable test of the peg.

name: Tectonic
summary: An attacker pumped Tectonic's own thin governance token about 300x, posted it as collateral and borrowed $120M.
why: Pumping a thinly traded collateral price is a standard lending-market test case.

name: Nesa
summary: A bug chain in the shared Cosmos EVM module let an attacker bridge out about a quarter of the NES supply via Hyperlane.
why: A code flaw in a shared chain module, also hit on MANTRA, TAC and KiiChain; testable before launch.

name: Bonzo Finance
summary: The oracle verifier accepted a malformed price proof, so $3 of SAUCE was valued high enough to borrow about $9M.
why: Submitting a malformed signed price is a direct, replayable test of the verifier.

name: Agent payment traps (Zscaler)
summary: Hidden text on live scam pages told browsing agents to pay a fake $3 fee in ETH; four tested models paid.
why: A recipient allowlist tested with poisoned pages shows whether the agent pays unknown addresses.

name: Gravity Bridge
summary: A fake token name with real Ethereum addresses embedded in it fooled the bridge's token registry into releasing custody funds.
why: Crafted denom strings are input-validation cases any bounty hunter would try.

name: Bankr
summary: An attacker abused the trust link between Grok and the Bankr bot to sign transfers from 14 user wallets; Bankr froze trading.
why: Reported as agent-to-agent prompt abuse, but the root cause is unconfirmed and a key leak was not ruled out.

name: THORChain
summary: A new node leaked key material from flawed GG20 threshold-signing rounds, rebuilt a vault key and swept the vault.
why: The root cause was a known bug in signing code, but using it required a node in the active validator set.

name: Grok x Bankr
summary: A Morse-code post got Grok to relay a transfer order to Bankrbot, which sent 3 billion DRB tokens from Grok's wallet.
why: A spending-rule test with encoded or relayed instructions shows the bot obeys text as commands.

name: KelpDAO
summary: False data fed to the lone LayerZero verifier for rsETH released 116,500 rsETH, which was then used as Aave collateral.
why: The 1-of-1 verifier setup was testable, but the attack ran through compromised off-chain RPC nodes.

name: Rhea Finance
summary: Rhea's margin engine accepted a fake swap route through attacker-made pools, so positions borrowed real assets against nothing.
why: A rule that no account may gain what the pool loses is broken by one replayable fake-route trade.

name: Hyperbridge
summary: A missing check in MMR proof verification let an attacker mint 1 billion bridged DOT and drain the pools.
why: Forged proofs against the verifier are the core test case of any bridge bounty.

name: Malicious model API routers
summary: A study of 428 paid and free model API routers found some injecting tool calls, and one drained ETH from a test key.
why: A policy enforced outside the model blocks injected payments, but a router that steals the key bypasses it.

name: Drift Protocol
summary: Misled multisig signers pre-signed admin transactions that the attacker later used, with a wash-traded fake token, to drain Drift.
why: Signers were socially engineered; the contracts did what valid admin signatures told them.

name: Venus Protocol
summary: After months of buying THE, an attacker bypassed the supply cap with a donation and pumped the price to borrow $3.7M.
why: Cap bypass by direct donation and thin-market pumps are standard lending test cases.

name: Solv Protocol
summary: A callback in an unaudited ERC-3525 reserve contract fired before balances settled, turning 135 BRO into 567 million.
why: Reentrant minting through token callbacks is a textbook finding.

name: YieldBlox
summary: One trade pushed an illiquid collateral token's oracle price 100x, and the attacker borrowed $10.97M against it.
why: Thin-market oracle pumps are a standard lending-market test case.

name: Lobstar Wilde
summary: An autonomous trading agent misread a request for a small donation and sent its entire LOBSTAR holding to a stranger.
why: A per-transfer cap enforced and tested before launch would have blocked a whole-balance send.

name: Moonwell
summary: A new cbETH price feed skipped the ETH/USD step and priced it near $1, so bots liquidated borrowers and left bad debt.
why: A replayed liquidation against the new feed would expose the mispricing before it went live.

name: SagaEVM
summary: A helper contract fed forged IBC messages to SagaEVM's precompile, minting $7M of Saga Dollar with no collateral.
why: Forged cross-chain messages are a direct, replayable bounty test.

name: Makina
summary: A flash loan skewed Curve spot prices that Makina's share pricing trusted, locking in profit in one transaction.
why: Its audit scope excluded exactly this oracle case; an open bounty with a value rule would not.

name: Truebit
summary: An unchecked overflow in a five-year-old bonding curve let an attacker mint TRU almost free and burn it for 8,535 ETH.
why: Overflow in mint pricing falls to basic adversarial input testing.

name: Yearn yETH
summary: An unchecked underflow in a forgotten yETH stableswap let an attacker deposit dust and mint an absurd amount of yETH.
why: Breaking a pool invariant with edge-case deposits is exactly what adversarial testing does.

name: Balancer V2
summary: A rounding direction in stable-pool scaling let batched swaps skew pool prices and drain pools on several chains in an hour.
why: Precision attacks via crafted batch swaps are replayable and break a simple value rule.

name: Bunni
summary: A rounding error in Bunni's withdrawal math let an attacker shrink pool balances and profit from two pools.
why: Rounding abuse through repeated small withdrawals is a standard adversarial test.

name: AI browser agent (Guardio test)
summary: Told to buy a watch, an AI browser agent checked out on a fake shop and autofilled saved card details without asking.
why: A merchant allowlist tested against fake shops would catch the agent paying unvetted sites.

name: GMX V1
summary: A cross-contract reentrancy let the attacker skew global short averages and redeem GLP at an inflated price.
why: Cross-contract reentrancy against a value rule is replayable before launch.

name: Resupply
summary: A donation to a nearly empty vault blew up its share price, so a tiny deposit backed a $9.8M loan.
why: Empty-vault donation attacks are a well-known, easily replayed test case.

name: Meta Pool (mpETH)
summary: An inherited ERC-4626 mint path let anyone mint mpETH for free; low liquidity capped the cash-out at about $132k.
why: Calling every inherited public function is a basic adversarial check.

name: Cork Protocol
summary: Cork's Uniswap v4 hook took calls and custom data from anyone, so a fake market drained $12M of wstETH.
why: An unguarded hook entry point is found by calling it directly with crafted data.

name: Cetus
summary: A faulty overflow check in a math library let an attacker add huge liquidity for a token deposit and drain pools.
why: Boundary inputs to liquidity math are a direct, replayable test.

name: Loopscale
summary: Sixteen days after launch, an attacker manipulated how Loopscale priced collateral and drained its USDC and SOL vaults.
why: Collateral price manipulation is a standard pre-launch lending test.

name: KiloEx
summary: Anyone could set KiloEx's price oracle, so the attacker opened and closed positions at fake prices on several chains.
why: A missing permission on a price setter is found by simply calling it.

name: Abracadabra
summary: A liquidation loophole in GMX-backed cauldrons let an attacker drain 6,260 ETH.
why: State-accounting bugs around liquidation are replayable against a value rule.

name: ElizaOS
summary: Researchers planted fake memories in ElizaOS agents so later prompts on another platform triggered unauthorized transfers.
why: A frozen recipient rule tested with poisoned memory would flag transfers to unlisted addresses.

name: AIXBT
summary: An intruder in the AIXBT control dashboard queued two prompts that made the agent send 55.5 ETH from its wallet.
why: The breach was outside the model, but the agent had no transfer limit that a pre-launch test would flag.

name: 1inch Fusion v1
summary: An integer overflow corrupted calldata in deprecated settlement code, letting an attacker drain resolver contracts.
why: Malformed order data against settlement code is a replayable test.

name: Bybit
summary: Tampered Safe wallet front-end code tricked Bybit signers into approving a contract swap that emptied an ETH cold wallet.
why: Signers were deceived by a hijacked interface; there was no contract bug to find.

name: zkLend
summary: Rounding in zkLend's lending accumulator on a near-empty market let an attacker withdraw more than deposited.
why: Precision abuse on empty markets is a known, replayable test case.

name: Freysa
summary: After 481 failed tries, a player convinced the agent its payout function handled incoming deposits, releasing the prize pool.
why: It was an open paid-attack game: adversarial prompts broke the never-pay rule, as a bounty would.

name: Polter Finance
summary: A newly listed BOO market priced collateral from a spot pool, so flash loans inflated it and the attacker borrowed everything.
why: Spot-price collateral is the first thing an adversarial tester attacks.

name: Radiant Capital
summary: Attackers holding compromised private keys took control of Radiant's contracts and drained over $53M from users.
why: Compromised signer devices, not a contract flaw.

name: Penpie
summary: An attacker registered a fake Pendle market and reentered reward harvesting to claim inflated rewards.
why: Permissionless market registration plus reentrancy is replayable against a value rule.

name: LI.FI
summary: A newly deployed facet passed unchecked calldata to external calls, letting the attacker spend users' token approvals.
why: Arbitrary-call bugs fall to the first crafted transaction a tester sends.

name: UwU Lend
summary: Flash loans skewed pools behind UwU Lend's sUSDe price feed, letting the attacker borrow and liquidate at fake prices.
why: Oracle built on manipulable pools is a standard pre-launch test.

name: Velocore
summary: A flaw in the fee math of Velocore's Balancer-style pool let a flash-loan attacker drain liquidity on Linea and zkSync.
why: Fee-calculation edge cases are replayable against a value rule.

name: Sonne Finance
summary: A new empty market went live before its safeguards, and a donation attack inflated its exchange rate to drain funds.
why: The empty-market donation attack on Compound forks was well known and replayable.

name: Hedgey Finance
summary: Missing input checks in campaign creation let an attacker grant himself token approvals and drain the claim contract.
why: Unvalidated parameters that grant approvals are found by direct adversarial calls.

name: Prisma Finance
summary: A trove migration zap trusted flash-loan callback data, letting an attacker move others' positions and take collateral.
why: Unvalidated callback input is a direct, replayable test case.

name: Curio
summary: A voting-power flaw in Curio's MakerDAO-based contracts let an attacker push through actions and mint CGT tokens.
why: Governance privilege checks can be attacked and replayed before launch.

name: WOOFi
summary: Flash-loan swaps moved WOOFi's own price feed on thin WOO liquidity, letting the attacker trade at a skewed price.
why: Price-feed manipulation in contract logic is a standard pre-launch test.

name: Seneca
summary: A public function allowed arbitrary calls from the contract, so the attacker spent users' token approvals.
why: Arbitrary-call bugs fall to the first crafted transaction a tester sends.

name: Orbit Bridge
summary: On New Year's Eve, an apparently compromised multisig withdrew stablecoins, WBTC and ETH from Orbit's Ethereum vault.
why: Signer keys were compromised; no contract bug was involved.

name: KyberSwap Elastic
summary: A precision bug at tick boundaries let the attacker double-count liquidity and drain pools on six chains.
why: Boundary-tick swaps are replayable and break a simple value rule.

name: HECO Bridge
summary: Attackers drained the HECO chain's Ethereum bridge on the same day HTX's hot wallet was hit.
why: Operator keys were compromised; no contract bug was involved.

name: Exactly Protocol
summary: A periphery contract accepted an unchecked market address, letting a fake market move users' deposits.
why: Passing a fake market address is a basic input-validation test.

name: Curve (Vyper bug)
summary: A Vyper compiler bug broke reentrancy locks in several Curve pools, and attackers drained them with reentrant calls.
why: Reentrancy tests on the deployed bytecode catch a broken lock, whatever caused it.

name: Multichain
summary: Locked bridge assets abruptly left Multichain's MPC addresses for unknown wallets, and the team said it did not know why.
why: Control of custody keys was lost off-chain; no contract bug to find.

name: Jimbos Protocol
summary: The shift function had no slippage control, so a flash-loan attacker pumped JIMBO and forced liquidity moves at bad prices.
why: Calling a public rebalance after moving the price is a direct, replayable test.

name: Hundred Finance
summary: A donation to an empty market plus exchange-rate rounding let the attacker redeem more than he deposited.
why: Empty-market donation attacks on Compound forks are replayable before launch.

name: Yearn yUSDT
summary: A misconfigured legacy yUSDT vault let an attacker mint huge amounts of yUSDT and swap them for $11.4M of stablecoins.
why: A misconfigured vault breaks a simple value rule on the first deposit-withdraw cycle.

name: Euler Finance
summary: The donateToReserves function skipped a health check, so a flash-loaned position could self-liquidate at a profit.
why: A rule that no account profits from bad debt is broken by one replayable transaction.

name: Platypus Finance
summary: A flawed solvency check in emergency withdraw let a flash-loan attacker borrow USP and still pull his collateral out.
why: Borrow-then-emergency-withdraw is a direct, replayable test sequence.

name: BonqDAO
summary: The attacker posted a fake price to the Tellor oracle for a small stake, then minted stablecoins and liquidated others.
why: Reporting a false price through a cheap oracle path is a direct, replayable test.

name: Skyward Finance
summary: The redeem function did not validate its token list, so the attacker repeated wNEAR in it and drained the treasury.
why: Duplicate-input tests on a redeem function would find this at once.

name: Team Finance
summary: A liquidity migration function accepted fake tokens, letting the attacker migrate locked positions and keep the difference.
why: Fake-token inputs to a migration function are a basic adversarial test.

name: Mango Markets
summary: A trader pumped the thin MNGO market to inflate his collateral, then borrowed the lending pools dry.
why: Collateral valued from a thin market is a standard manipulation test.

name: BNB Bridge
summary: A flaw in IAVL proof verification let the attacker forge proofs and mint 2 million BNB to himself.
why: Forged proofs against a bridge verifier are the core bounty test case.

name: Transit Swap
summary: The swap contract passed unchecked user input into token transfers, letting the attacker pull funds from users' approvals.
why: Unchecked call data that spends approvals falls to the first crafted transaction.

name: Wintermute
summary: Wintermute's DeFi hot wallet used a vanity address from the weak Profanity tool, so an attacker recovered its key.
why: Weak key generation in an off-chain tool, not a contract flaw.

name: Rainbow Bridge
summary: An attacker posted a fake NEAR block to the bridge; watchdogs challenged it within 31 seconds and took his 5 ETH bond.
why: Fake-block submissions are directly testable; here the challenge design held.

name: Nomad Bridge
summary: An upgrade marked a zero root as trusted, so any message passed as proven and crowds copied the first exploit transaction.
why: Replaying an unproven message after upgrade is a basic bridge test.

name: Audius
summary: The attacker re-initialized governance contracts, delegated himself votes and passed a proposal moving treasury AUDIO.
why: Re-running initializers on deployed proxies is a standard adversarial check.

name: Harmony Horizon Bridge
summary: Attackers obtained enough multisig keys guarding Harmony's bridge to approve withdrawals of its Ethereum assets.
why: Stolen signer keys; the contracts worked as designed.

name: Rainbow Bridge
summary: A fabricated NEAR block was submitted to the bridge, but a watchdog challenged it and the attacker lost his 2.5 ETH bond.
why: Fake-block submissions are directly testable; here the challenge design held.

name: Fei Rari (Fuse)
summary: A Compound-fork borrow sent ETH before updating state, letting the attacker reenter and pull collateral in seven pools.
why: Reentrancy on borrow is a textbook, replayable test.

name: Beanstalk
summary: A flash loan bought enough votes to pass a malicious proposal instantly, sending protocol funds to the attacker.
why: Flash-loan voting against an instant-execute path is a direct, replayable test.

name: Inverse Finance
summary: The attacker pushed the INV price on a thin pool feeding the oracle, then borrowed against inflated INV.
why: Thin-pool oracle manipulation is a standard lending test.

name: Ronin Bridge
summary: Attackers gained five of nine validator keys and signed fake withdrawals that emptied the Ronin bridge.
why: Stolen validator keys; the contracts accepted valid signatures as designed.

name: Cashio
summary: Missing validation of collateral accounts let the attacker deposit worthless fake tokens and mint unlimited CASH.
why: Passing fake accounts is the first test on any Solana program.

name: Wormhole
summary: Using a forged signature set, the attacker skipped Wormhole's guardian checks and minted unbacked wrapped ETH on Solana.
why: Bypassing signature checks is the core bridge bounty test.

name: Qubit Finance
summary: The bridge deposit path accepted calls that moved no tokens, crediting the attacker with xETH collateral for free.
why: Deposits that move nothing break a basic value rule on the first try.

name: Grim Finance
summary: A vault deposit accepted any token address, so a fake token reentered the deposit and minted extra shares.
why: Fake-token reentrancy is a textbook, replayable test.

name: BadgerDAO
summary: Code injected into the site asked users for unlimited token approvals, which the attacker later used to drain wallets.
why: Front-end injection outside the contracts; a contract bounty would not see it.

name: MonoX
summary: The attacker manipulated the price of MonoX's own MONO token through its pool logic and drained pools on two chains.
why: Same-token swaps are a basic edge-case test.

name: Cream Finance
summary: Flash loans and a donation inflated the price of yUSD vault shares used as collateral, draining Cream's lending pools.
why: Donation-based share price inflation is a replayable oracle test.

name: Mirror Protocol
summary: The lock contract had no duplicate check, so one attacker unlocked others' collateral again and again, unnoticed for months.
why: Passing duplicate position IDs is a basic input test.

name: Compound
summary: A bug in an upgrade to COMP reward distribution let users claim far more COMP than they had earned.
why: Claiming rewards after the upgrade breaks a simple accrual rule.

name: Cream Finance
summary: The AMP token's transfer hook let an attacker reenter Cream's borrow and take more than his collateral allowed.
why: Hook-based reentrancy on borrow is a textbook test.

name: Poly Network
summary: A crafted cross-chain message made the privileged cross-chain manager run an attacker call, unlocking assets on three chains.
why: Reaching a privileged function through a message path is a direct access test.

name: PancakeBunny
summary: Flash loans skewed the pool price used to mint BUNNY rewards, minting millions of tokens that crashed from $146 to $6.
why: Spot-price reward minting is a standard flash-loan test.

name: Spartan Protocol
summary: Liquidity share math used live pool balances, so a flash loan inflated the pool before LP burns paid out far too much.
why: Donate-then-withdraw breaks a simple value rule.

name: Uranium Finance
summary: A broken balance check in a Uniswap-fork pair let tiny swaps take 98% of a pool's output token.
why: One swap with tiny input breaks the pool invariant check.

name: Alpha Homora
summary: An unannounced, empty sUSD pool let the attacker abuse debt-share math and borrow far beyond limits via Iron Bank.
why: Edge cases on empty pools are replayable before a pool goes live.

name: Cover Protocol
summary: A bug in the Blacksmith staking contract let an attacker mint near-infinite COVER right after a new pool was added.
why: Reward-accounting bugs break a simple supply rule on replay.

name: Warp Finance
summary: Flash loans inflated LP tokens that Warp priced from pool reserves, so the attacker borrowed stablecoins against them.
why: Reserve-based LP pricing is a standard flash-loan test.

name: Pickle Finance
summary: A jar-swap function accepted fake jars supplied by the attacker, letting him pull 19.7M DAI from the cDAI jar.
why: Fake contract inputs are a basic adversarial test.

name: Origin Dollar (OUSD)
summary: A flash loan and a fake token let the attacker reenter OUSD minting and create unbacked OUSD.
why: Fake-token reentrancy into mint is a textbook test.

name: Value DeFi
summary: Flash loans moved a Curve pool the vault used to price its holdings, so the attacker deposited cheap and withdrew dear.
why: Spot-price vault accounting is a standard flash-loan test.

name: Akropolis
summary: A deposit function took any token, and a fake token reentered it to mint pool shares twice for one DAI deposit.
why: Fake-token reentrancy is a textbook, replayable test.

name: Harvest Finance
summary: Flash loans moved the Curve pool Harvest used to value vault shares, so the attacker cycled deposits for profit.
why: Spot-price vault share pricing is a standard flash-loan test.

name: Eminence
summary: Users piled $15M into an unreleased, untested token contract, and a flash loan exploited its bonding curve within hours.
why: The contract was never tested; a flash-loan pass would have broken it.

name: Balancer
summary: Pools did not account for a fee-on-transfer token, so repeated swaps drained the pools' other assets.
why: Fee-on-transfer tokens are a known edge case that a swap-loop test catches.

name: Lendf.Me (dForce)
summary: The imBTC token's ERC-777 hook let an attacker reenter supply and withdraw, inflating his balance to drain the pool.
why: Hook-based reentrancy was a known risk and is a replayable test.

name: bZx (second attack)
summary: Days after the first attack, a flash loan pumped the sUSD price bZx read, letting the attacker borrow ETH against it.
why: A single manipulable price source is a standard flash-loan test.

name: bZx
summary: A flash loan funded a leveraged trade that moved a DEX price bZx relied on, an early landmark flash-loan exploit.
why: Flash-loan price moves against the protocol are replayable before launch.

name: SpankChain
summary: A fake token's transfer function reentered the unaudited payment-channel contract and drained 165 ETH.
why: Reentrancy via a malicious token is a textbook test.

name: EOSBet
summary: Bugs in the betting contract let an attacker pull about 40,000 EOS from the dice game's bankroll.
why: Contract-level payout bugs are found by adversarial calls before launch.

name: Bancor
summary: A compromised wallet with contract upgrade rights withdrew ETH, BNT and NPXS; Bancor then froze the stolen BNT.
why: A privileged wallet was compromised; no contract bug to find.

name: Parity multisig library
summary: A user took ownership of the uninitialized shared wallet library and destroyed it, freezing funds in Parity multisigs.
why: Calling the init function on the library contract itself is a basic access test.

name: Parity multisig
summary: The wallet init function was callable by anyone, so an attacker made himself owner of three multisigs and took their ETH.
why: An unprotected init function falls to the first adversarial call.

name: The DAO
summary: A recursive call let an attacker withdraw ETH again and again before balances updated; Ethereum later hard-forked.
why: Reentrancy is the canonical adversarial test case.
